title: Plan Lent
hook: one thing to give up, one to take up
tomorrow: after Easter Sunday, why keep celebrating for weeks?

segments.voice: Yesterday, plan Advent: a road built before the traveler comes. Your line was prepare the way. Today, the other season of getting ready.

Chocolate. Social media. The snooze button. Those are the classic answers when someone asks what you're giving up for Lent. But a plan that only subtracts leaves a gap. What fills the space where the chocolate used to be? Lent, at its best, is a trade: one thing out, one thing in.
screen: `CHOCOLATE? SOCIAL MEDIA?` → `SUBTRACTING LEAVES A GAP.` → `ONE THING OUT, ONE THING IN.`

segments.voice: The question underneath: what is a season of going-without for? Lent is the season before Easter, and tradition ties it to Jesus in the wilderness, where Matthew says he fasted forty days and forty nights. Some churches open it with ashes on Ash Wednesday; others mark it more quietly. For the plan itself, Matthew 6 is the place to look: Jesus sets three practices side by side, giving, praying and fasting, and asks that each be kept between a person and God. The prophet Joel says what all three are aiming at, in the King James Bible: “And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God.” Tearing your clothes was an outward sign of grief. Joel asks for the inside to turn. So a Lent plan has two halves. Less: one thing set down. More: one thing taken up. The less makes room; the more fills it. Now a neighbor. Muslims fast in the month of Ramadan, and the Qur'an says fasting is prescribed for believers as it was prescribed for those before them, so that they may guard themselves against evil. Shared ground: a season of fasting meant to turn a person toward God, a season the Qur'an itself says others kept before. An honest difference: for Muslims, Ramadan's fast is commanded in the Qur'an, from first light until nightfall, all month. For Christians, Lent is a church season, and churches keep it in different ways.
screen: `WHAT IS GOING-WITHOUT FOR?` · `GIVE, PRAY, FAST, IN SECRET.` · `REND YOUR HEART: TURN.` · `A NEIGHBOR: THE RAMADAN FAST.` · then, large: `LESS AND MORE.`

segments.voice: Hold out both hands. Turn one palm down, as if setting something on a table, and name the one thing you'd put down for Lent. Turn the other palm up, as if receiving, and name the one thing you'd take up: a gift, a prayer, a kindness. Hold both hands still until the sit ends.
Plan Lent. One thing to give up, one to take up, both aimed at a turned heart, and decided before the season starts.
Carry this: less and more, a palm down and a palm up. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: my college roommate is Layla! she says she fasts for ramadan in spring. is that like lent?
options: Some is shared: a fast to turn toward God. But it's its own thing. Ask her about it.
Same thing, different name. Every religion's fasting is basically identical.
Not at all. Lent's Christian, Ramadan's Muslim, so there's nothing shared.
chat.meaning: Both are seasons of fasting meant to turn a person toward God. Ramadan's fast is commanded in the Qur'an; Lent is a church season kept in many ways.
